reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Most cases are caused by de novo variants in ATP1A3, encoding a neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase subunit that maintains ion gradients and neuronal excitability
Onset is before 18 months of age with recurrent episodes of hemiplegia that alternate sides, and attacks affecting both sides can cause quadriparesis
A hallmark is that the hemiplegic and other paroxysmal attacks resolve with sleep and may resume on waking
Additional paroxysmal features include abnormal eye movements (including monocular nystagmus), tonic or dystonic attacks and autonomic disturbance
Most children develop progressive cognitive impairment, developmental delay, persistent dystonia and epilepsy over time
ATP1A3 variants underlie an overlapping spectrum that also includes rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and the CAPOS syndrome
Management emphasises trigger avoidance and agents such as flunarizine to reduce attack frequency and severity, alongside supportive care
reference.pathophysiology: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is usually caused by de novo missense variants in ATP1A3, which encodes the alpha-3 subunit of the neuronal sodium-potassium ATPase responsible for restoring transmembrane ion gradients after neuronal firing. Impaired pump function disturbs neuronal repolarisation and raises susceptibility to episodic dysfunction, producing paroxysmal hemiplegia, dystonia and oculomotor disturbance that are relieved by the reduced metabolic demand of sleep. Repeated episodes and chronic pump dysfunction are associated with progressive neurological and cognitive decline, and the same gene produces a phenotypic spectrum spanning rapid-onset dystonia-parkinsonism and CAPOS syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Focal epilepsy with recurrent Todd paresis
Recurrent stroke or vasculopathy in childhood
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with vascular imaging to exclude structural and vascular causes
Electroencephalography, ideally ictal, to characterise attacks and detect coexisting epilepsy
Metabolic screen including lactate and CSF/blood glucose ratio for GLUT1 deficiency
Echocardiography and cardiac monitoring given reported arrhythmia risk
redFlags: Prolonged or bilateral attacks causing respiratory or bulbar compromise
Status epilepticus in a child with coexisting epilepsy
Cardiac arrhythmia or sudden unexplained deterioration
reference.prognosis: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is a serious disorder with a generally guarded outlook; although individual hemiplegic attacks resolve, most children accumulate cognitive impairment, dystonia and epilepsy over time. Attack frequency may lessen with treatment such as flunarizine, but long-term neurological disability is common.
pitfalls: Mistaking early attacks for hemiplegic migraine or focal seizures and delaying ATP1A3 testing
Failing to note that resolution with sleep is a key diagnostic clue
Overlooking coexisting epilepsy, which requires separate assessment and treatment
Neglecting cardiac surveillance given the recognised arrhythmia risk in the ATP1A3 spectrum
